name: Adam Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the machining cell at Brennan Pumps, on the early shift. Six CNC machines, mostly lathes and two milling centres, cutting pump housings and impellers out of cast iron and bronze. I start at six, read the handover notes, check the tool wear on every machine and then spend the day making sure the parts come off inside the tolerance, which on an impeller is a few hundredths of a millimetre. I've been there fourteen years and I lead a team of five.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part of the day, and the worst?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is when a tricky first-off part comes out right and the inspector, Ruth, can't find anything to write down. The worst is when a machine throws an alarm at half past five and nobody on nights left a note. Lately I've started pasting the alarm codes into one of those AI chat apps on my phone, and it's right maybe two times in three, which is better than the manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that matches what I see. It's handy for alarm codes and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and nothing more, like when we got the first touch-screen controllers. I'd tell the lads to stop worrying and keep their skills sharp. Online I'd probably share some article about how the bosses oversold it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I'm good at what I do and in this picture that keeps counting. It also means the next pay talks are about pay, not about who's being replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. Keep using the phone app for alarm codes and the odd handover note. Leila and I would stick to the plan of overpaying the mortgage a little each month and keeping about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I already know how to work in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI for alarm codes. Would you push it further if it stayed this modest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit, once I saw it working for others. Ruth's started using it to write her inspection reports and they're cleaner than mine. If she shows me how, I'd try it, but I'm not going to be the first one to bet a shift on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Brennan would be most relieved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mick on the big lathe, who's fifty-eight and counting days to his pension. He asks me every month whether the robots are coming. In this one I'd tell him, Mick, you're safe, go and buy that caravan.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a useful tool and nothing more, like the first touch-screen controllers, tell his team to keep their skills sharp, and share an article about bosses overselling it.
S0.think: He'd be glad, because his skill keeps counting and pay talks stay about pay rather than about who gets replaced.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, using the phone app for alarm codes and handover notes. Keeps overpaying the mortgage a little each month and holds about four months of savings.
S0.feel: Calm, in a world he already knows how to work in.
S0.quote: I'm not going to be the first one to bet a shift on it.
S0.fieldNote: Adam already uses AI in a small, practical way and judges it by results: right two times in three. He waits for proof from colleagues like Ruth before going further. His first thought for others goes to Mick, which shows the team-lead instinct.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can picture. The robot loading cells are already at the trade fairs every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is fine as long as it's shared. If a robot loads my lathes, the time it saves should mean shorter shifts or better pay, not five fewer people. I'd say that at the union meeting, and I'd say it to management on the safety committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right. Somebody has to set up and program the cell, and I'm the one who knows these machines. But I think the team goes from five to three, and I'd be the one standing there when they tell the other two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Brennan to put me on the robot programming course the supplier runs, once the first cell is working. I'd back the union pushing for a deal that moves people, not drops them. At home, we'd build the savings from four months to six over a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much, but for my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the two who'd be let go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth before the office does, because that's the least they're owed. And I'd ring round the other shops in the area, there are three or four machine shops within half an hour. Good machinists still get picked up, at least for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the course once the first cell is working. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen kit come in that never worked. We had a measuring probe system four years ago that sat in a corner for a year. I'm happy to learn, but I want to see it cut a decent part first.

S1.say: He'd say change is fine if it's shared: time saved by robots should mean shorter shifts or better pay, not fewer people. He'd raise it at the union and the safety committee.
S1.think: He thinks he'd be fine, as the one who knows the machines and could program the cell, but expects his team to shrink from five to three and dreads telling the others.
S1.do: Asks Brennan to send him on the supplier's robot programming course once the first cell works. Backs a union deal that moves people rather than drops them, and builds savings from four months to six.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly for his team rather than himself.
S1.quote: I'd tell them the truth before the office does, because that's the least they're owed.
S1.fieldNote: Adam's personal outlook is fairly secure here, and his worry is pointed at the people he leads. He'll learn the new thing, but only after seeing it cut a decent part, a wait shaped by a failed probe system years ago. He'd use both the union and his own phone list of nearby shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. That's two pay rounds away. That's before Sara starts secondary school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs the government in, properly, like in a war or a pandemic. Wage support, a pause on repossessions, and the companies paying in. I'd be at the union march, and I'd be telling everyone at work to join if they hadn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd lose the job within a year of it arriving. If the robot can program itself and check its own parts, then the thing that makes me valuable is gone. I've got maybe four months of money. Leila's job might hold on longer, nurses usually do, but we can't pay the mortgage on her pay alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the mortgage overpayments right away and start saving everything into the account. We'd drop the second car and the kids' trip with the school. I'd join a campaign for wage support. If Brennan let people go, I'd take any work going while it lasted, even back on a manual lathe at some jobbing shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake running the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car, then the holiday. Then probably Noah's football club fees, which would break my heart because he's actually good. We'd keep the internet, because the kids need it for school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning let you do, compared with nothing at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. It's enough to save a bit and get the family ready for a hard time. It's not enough to learn a new trade and get established in it. Two years is a warning, not a plan.

S2.say: He'd call for government action on the scale of a war or pandemic: wage support, a pause on repossessions and companies paying in. He'd march with the union and urge colleagues to join.
S2.think: He expects to lose his job within a year of AGI arriving, since the robots would program and check themselves. With four months saved and Leila's pay alone not covering the mortgage, the family would be exposed.
S2.do: Stops mortgage overpayments and saves everything. Drops the second car and the school trip, joins a wage-support campaign, and takes any work going, even on a manual lathe at a jobbing shop.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake running the numbers.
S2.quote: Two years is a warning, not a plan.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture overturns the security Adam felt in the steady one, because AGI removes exactly the programming skill he was counting on. He thinks in household budgets, naming the cuts in order down to Noah's football club. His public line is big and political, but his private one is a quiet sum on the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be forty-eight. It's still a shock, but you can at least turn the ship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them: retraining paid for now, not after people are out of work. I'd be pushing the union and our local council on it. I'd tell people at work to start thinking about what comes next, without panicking them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have three good years and then a hard two. That's enough to clear a chunk of the mortgage and get Noah through school. I'd also start looking at what jobs still need a person in the room, because I don't think machining is one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put six months of money aside, and I'd start an evening course, maybe electrical installation, since I've got the technical diploma already. I'd talk to Leila about whether she goes up to full time. I'd stay at Brennan as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical installation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because houses will still need wiring done in odd old buildings for a while, and that's fiddly work. My brother-in-law Sami is an electrician and he's always saying he can't find people. I don't know if it'd last, but it'd last longer than standing at a lathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay at Brennan as long as they'd have you. Isn't that leaving it late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'm not walking away from a steady wage with two kids and a mortgage to bet on something I've not proven yet. I'd do the course alongside, and jump when Sami's got enough work for me. That's how I do things.

S3.say: He'd say there are a few years, so retraining should be paid for now, not after people lose work, and he'd push the union and local council while telling colleagues to think ahead calmly.
S3.think: He expects three good years and then a hard two, enough to clear some mortgage and get Noah through school, and he'd look for jobs that still need a person in the room.
S3.do: Builds six months of savings in the first year and starts an evening electrical installation course. Talks to Leila about going full time and stays at Brennan until his brother-in-law Sami has enough work for him.
S3.feel: Anxious, but helped by having something to do.
S3.quote: I'm not walking away from a steady wage with two kids and a mortgage to bet on something I've not proven yet.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Adam do things his steady way: learn on the side, move only once the new path is proven. His plan rests on a real person, his brother-in-law Sami, rather than on a scheme. He's honest that he doesn't know if electrical work would last, only that it would last longer than machining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Noah would be twenty-four, Sara twenty. The mortgage would be nearly gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get this right, if we start now. Shorter working weeks, a share of the profits for the people being replaced, and free training. I'd be pushing that through the union, and voting for whoever took it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes it something I can plan for. I'd be fifty-three when it arrives, with the house nearly paid and the kids grown. It's not comfortable, but I think we'd come through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Brennan and do the electrical course at a gentler pace over two or three years. I'd keep the savings at about six months and keep overpaying the mortgage so it's done by the time it hits. I'd encourage the younger lads on my team to start looking now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's more like weather you can see coming than a storm on top of you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between five years and ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five, I'm squeezing a new trade into a few evenings while panicking a bit. With ten, I can do it properly and still have time to see if the new trade itself gets swallowed. Time to look before I jump, which is how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noah about his own plans, with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to just pick something because it pays now. Pick something where people trust a person to do it, and learn the machines that'll do the rest. He wants to be a mechanic, and I'd tell him to do it, but to learn the diagnostic software as well.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is enough to get this right if work starts now: shorter weeks, profit-sharing for replaced workers and free training, pushed through the union and at the ballot box.
S4.think: Privately ten years makes it something he can plan for. He'd be 53, with the house nearly paid and the children grown, and he thinks the family would come through.
S4.do: Keeps working at Brennan and does the electrical course over two or three years. Holds savings at about six months, keeps overpaying the mortgage, and encourages younger team members to start looking now.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steady, like weather you can see coming.
S4.quote: Time to look before I jump, which is how I like it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years suits Adam's style exactly: he can test the new trade before committing. His advice to Noah, choose work where people trust a person, shows how he sorts jobs in his head. The policy demands stay the same across the AGI pictures; only his private worry falls as time grows.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the only one where I can't see a sensible next step. What would help is wage support that kicks in straight away, not after three months of forms, and somebody making the banks hold off on mortgages while people find their feet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what skilled people are worth in all this. I've spent fourteen years getting to where I can hear a lathe chatter and know the tool's going. That's real knowledge. If it's all going into a machine, I'd like it written down somewhere that we taught it, because nobody's going to put our names on the robot.

headlineQuote: I can hear a lathe chatter and know the tool's going.
portrait: Adam Silva is 43 and leads the early-shift machining cell at Brennan Pumps, cutting pump housings and impellers on six CNC machines. He uses an AI app on his phone for alarm codes but waits for proof before trying anything bigger. He stays calm or uneasy in the slower pictures, where his programming skill still counts, but becomes alarmed when AGI arrives in two years and that skill no longer protects him. With five or ten years, he plans an evening electrical course and a move to his brother-in-law's trade, but only once it's proven. He backs the union and public wage support throughout, and worries most for the people he leads.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it's the only one where he can't see a sensible next step.
whatWouldHelp: Wage support that starts straight away without months of forms, and banks being made to hold off on mortgages while people find their feet.
